reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-five home runs projected at age 23 is the headline, and the contact profile underneath it isn't inflating that number. An average exit velocity of 92.7 mph and a 50.1% hard-hit rate explain the .504 xSLG; the barrel rate at 13.4% is the kind of frequency that holds up over a full season. What makes him genuinely interesting is that the walk rate sits at 12.2% while the strikeout rate is only 18.8%, a combination that produces the .358 OBP and pushes the projection toward .895 OPS across 701 plate appearances. The defensive profile is a liability and the sprint speed is below average, so if the bat ever goes sideways he doesn't have another tool to lean on — but right now this is a middle-of-the-order bat already operating like one of the better offensive third basemen in the American League.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xwOBA and xSLG are elite-tier, .362 and .474, but paired with a 27.1% strikeout rate that sits near the bottom of the league. That gap is the whole profile: a hitter who barrels the ball at a 12.7% clip and draws walks at 11.8%, yet chases at 33.8%, which is why the actual batting average lags behind what the contact quality deserves. Crow-Armstrong is a true five-category threat if the chase rate stays manageable, with a projection of 37 home runs, 39 steals, and a .899 OPS across 713 plate appearances. If the swing decisions erode, the strikeouts eat into enough at-bats that the power and speed still play but the OBP craters and the overall value drops a tier.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact quality is easy to trust — 92.6 mph average exit velocity, 13.1% barrel rate, and an xSLG that matches his projected .487 SLG almost exactly, but the profile has a real crack in it. His 35.6% chase rate and 30.5% whiff rate sit near the bottom of the league, and those aren't numbers that coexist peacefully with a .282 projection unless the hard contact keeps overwhelming the swing decisions. If the plate discipline doesn't improve, the strikeouts eat into the AVG and the 7.7% walk rate offers no cushion. When it holds together, this is a 30-homer, 21-steal outfielder with middle-of-the-order production, the kind of profile that doesn't need refinement to be valuable, just consistency.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The xwOBA split is what makes him singular: .410 as a hitter, .257 as a pitcher, both sitting 94th percentile or better. At the plate, a 16.7% barrel rate and 93.5 mph average exit velocity explain why the projection calls for 39 home runs and a .947 OPS across 689 plate appearances, and a 13.2% walk rate gives him enough margin that the 23.0% strikeout rate doesn't bite. On the mound, a 2.72 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate backed by a 98.1 mph fastball show a genuine ace alongside the DH role. The one dependency worth naming is workload management — everything here assumes he holds up doing both jobs for a full Dodger season, and if injury forces a choice, you're still getting an elite player, just half the profile.

His 47.3% hard-hit rate and xSLG of .468, both well above the median, sit underneath a projected 25-home-run, 28-steal season that fits the contact quality. reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The .857 OPS projection sits on a contact profile that's genuinely messier underneath than the surface number suggests. His xSLG of .447 and xwOBA of .342 grade comfortably above average, but a 37.2% chase rate that ranks in the 13th percentile is a real liability, and the 29.2% whiff rate explains why pitchers keep going there. The power and speed combination, 35 projected home runs and 31 stolen bases, is what lifts this profile from good-not-great into something worth paying for at shortstop. The whole thing hinges on whether plate discipline tightens enough to stop suppressing his floor, because if the chase rate sticks where it is, the .272 average fades and you're left with a boom-or-bust contributor rather than the rounded everyday player the projection describes.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact quality here is elite, but the strikeout rate is the whole argument. An average exit velocity of 93.8 mph and a 51.5% hard-hit rate put him in legitimately rare company, and the underlying expected numbers, .358 xwOBA and .469 xSLG, suggest the projection's .815 OPS undersells what he's capable of when he makes contact. The problem is a 27.2% strikeout rate that claws back a big chunk of that value, because all that exit velocity doesn't score if pitchers can consistently put him away. If he trims the whiff rate even modestly, the 26 home runs and 30 stolen bags in the projection start to look like a floor rather than a ceiling; if pitchers keep finding the hole in his swing, he's a volatile, exciting, second-division-regular type rather than the star the ball-in-play numbers imply.

reports.name: Yordan Alvarez
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .461 and the xSLG is .681, and those aren't separated by much daylight from what the projection expects him to actually do. A .316/.430/.609 slash with 45 home runs in 690 plate appearances is the projection, and the contact quality underneath it, 94.5 mph average exit velocity, 17.7% barrel rate, 53.4% hard-hit rate, shows a hitter whose damage is both frequent and severe. His 15.9% walk rate does as much work as the raw power, because pitchers can't live on the edges without paying for it, and a 16.8% strikeout rate means he's almost never giving an at-bat away free. The sprint speed is where it ends, at 25.1 ft/s, but for a DH whose entire profile runs through contact quality and plate discipline, that's barely a footnote.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The .419 xwOBA and .585 xSLG are both at the top of the sport, and they're built on a 20.8% barrel rate and 95.1 mph average exit velocity that leave no doubt about the underlying contact quality. The one live wire in the profile is a 28.6% strikeout rate, and the bet Wood is making, successfully so far, is that a 16.8% walk rate keeps enough plate appearances from ending in outs that the strikeouts don't drain what the power produces. If pitchers ever find a consistent way to exploit that 30.7% whiff rate, the walk rate is what keeps him from sliding into a boom-or-bust corner type; if they don't, the projection's .388 OBP and 35 home runs are a floor, not a ceiling.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is almost absurdly clean at the contact end: 52.6% hard-hit rate and a .288 xBA that both sit comfortably in the top tier, and the .365 xWOBA says the quality is genuine and sustained. What the profile isn't, and what keeps the projection at .787 OPS rather than something louder, is a disciplined one. A 27.2% whiff rate limits how much of that raw contact quality actually scores, and the projection's .433 SLG trails the .462 xSLG by enough to matter. The 36 projected steals are the wild card that keeps his overall value whole even in seasons where the power doesn't fully translate, and if the whiff rate hardens into a floor rather than a work-in-progress, you're still looking at a plus-speed, plus-contact outfielder with real pop: a genuine everyday player, just not the MVP-tier one the exit velocity alone would suggest.

reports.name: Kevin McGonigle
reports.published_report: A 19.1% chase rate ranks in the 98th percentile, and that's not a quirk of the profile — it's the engine. McGonigle's plate discipline is genuinely elite: his 14.1% walk rate matches his 14.1% strikeout rate exactly, a balance almost no one achieves, and the .350 xwOBA reflects that he's extracting value from contact even though the raw exit velocity at 88.1 mph sits well below average. The power ceiling is bounded, with a .423 xSLG suggesting solid but not special thump, and the projection's 17 home runs across a full 700-PA season feels like the realistic ceiling of that profile, not a floor. Everything here hinges on whether that zone command holds as pitchers continue to map him; if the chase rate drifts toward ordinary, the .280 average and .381 OBP collapse together, and what's left is a glove-first infielder without enough pop to carry the bat.

reports.name: Andy Pages
reports.published_report: The gap between his .340 xwOBA and his 88.9 mph average exit velocity is the whole puzzle with Pages: the contact quality shows up in the expected numbers, but the raw velo reads ordinary, which means he's getting there through elite contact placement rather than brute force. His xBA sits at .271 with a chase rate of 32.0%, which is aggressive, but a 22.2% whiff rate suggests he's making enough contact on pitches he offers at to keep the strikeout rate at a manageable 19.5%. Add 28.3 ft/s sprint speed and fielding that grades at the 95th percentile, and the projection's 27 home runs with 15 steals across 681 plate appearances starts to look less like optimism than like a reasonable ceiling for a profile that contributes in every column. The hinge is whether that contact placement holds up against tighter sequencing — if pitchers find the weak quadrant and the exit velo tells the real story, you get a solid fourth outfielder; if the xBA translates, he's a legitimately above-average regular in one of the best lineups in baseball.

reports.name: Kade Anderson

Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: A 36.9% chase rate sits in rarefied air, and paired with a 5.6% walk rate, it explains everything about why Sánchez works. Hitters swing at his stuff outside the zone constantly and make contact when they do connect, but the contact is soft enough at 89.3 mph average exit velo that it hasn't hurt him yet — where the Statcast card gets complicated is a 41.8% hard-hit rate that runs well below the median for good pitchers, suggesting his xERA of 3.34 is closer to his true talent than a 2.59 projection ERA implies. The profile hinges entirely on that chase rate holding: if hitters start laying off, the strikeout rate (27.8%) erodes and there isn't premium velocity to fall back on. If the chase stays, he's a legitimate mid-rotation horse worth every bit of 205.8 innings.

reports.name: Miguel Sime Jr.
reports.published_report: Sixteen strikeouts per nine innings at A & A+ is the loudest number in the 2026 minor leagues, and Sime's 118 punchouts across 65.3 innings have him sitting at the 99th percentile among pitchers in his pool. The problem lives right next to it: 58 walks in that same sample, a BB/9 of 8.0 that translates to 7.0 in MLB-equivalent terms against a league context where MLB arms average 3.2. That K-BB% of 21 across A+ & A reads elite in the minors, but the translation collapses it to 12.6, just short of the MLB average of 13.5. The whole profile hinges on whether the command develops enough to let the strikeout stuff breathe — if it does, there's a rotation piece in there somewhere; if the walks travel with him, he's a depth arm and that's the ceiling the data already names.

reports.name: Zebby Matthews
reports.published_report: The fastball sits 95.2 mph and the walk rate is a passable 7.8%, so the surface reads fine — the problem is everything hitters do once they decide to swing. A 21.9% whiff rate and 27.5% chase rate both land in the bottom quarter of the league, which means contact isn't a byproduct of bad luck; barrels are finding him at an 11.6% clip, and average exit velocity of 90.6 mph confirms it. The xERA of 4.69 and a projected 5.05 ERA across 120.3 innings tell the same story from two angles: he can eat innings and probably will, but not as a rotation piece you trust in a meaningful spot. If the chase rate lifts even modestly he becomes a back-end arm who earns his spot; if it stays where it is now, he's a guy who gives Minnesota bulk while they wait for something better.

reports.name: Byron Buxton
reports.published_report: A 16.9% barrel rate is nearly impossible to sustain — except Buxton's whole Statcast profile says the power isn't going anywhere. The .496 xSLG sits at the 92nd percentile, the barrel rate at the 98th, and the projection's .519 SLG lands right where you'd expect given that contact quality. The catch is the chase and whiff numbers: a 34.3% chase rate and 31.7% whiff rate drag the xBA down to .247, which is why the projection's .255 AVG and 7.1% walk rate frame him as a slugger who earns his counting stats the hard way, not a balanced offensive force. If he plays 519 plate appearances, 33 home runs is a reasonable expectation from a player who barrels the ball this consistently; if the knee or hamstring cuts that to 350, the ceiling collapses into something a lot less exciting.

At A-ball, Castro has issued 28 walks in 77.3 innings, a 3.3 BB/9 that ranks at the 81st percentile among his peers — the command is genuinely ahead of his age. reports.name: Sammy Hernandez
reports.published_report: The .438 OBP and .271 ISO at A+ are genuinely difficult to dismiss, even at 194 plate appearances, because the discipline and the pop are moving together rather than trading off. Sammy Hernandez has walked 34 times against 34 strikeouts this season, an 18% clip on each side, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his walk rate at 11.4% while the mlb_avg sits at 8.5% — the plate discipline carries through the filter. The power translates to a .167 ISO equivalent, roughly matching what the average big-league hitter puts up, so the ceiling compresses fast: the A+ numbers are loud, but if it works he becomes a bench or platoon catcher, not a lineup fixture. The profile hinges on whether he holds this contact rate as pitching gets craftier, because a catcher who walks at that rate and makes this kind of contact is a real roster asset, and one who doesn't is depth.

reports.name: Jared Serna
reports.published_report: The contact is actually the carrying tool here — 48 strikeouts in 303 AAA plate appearances translates to a 19% K rate at the MLB level, below a league average that sits at 22%, and that discipline is the one thing keeping this profile afloat. The problem is everything else. A .221 average sitting on a .231 BABIP leaves almost no margin, the ISO at AAA is .148 with a .131 MLB-equivalent, and a 17th-percentile OBP among his peer pool says the contact isn't turning into baserunners at anything like an acceptable rate. Fourteen stolen bases add a real dimension, and 30 walks show genuine feel for the zone, but the power won't carry a lineup spot and the batting average floor is already cracking. If the BABIP normalizes upward and the contact skill plays at the big-league level as cleanly as it does in translation, he's a useful bench piece; if it doesn't, he's organizational depth who strikes out less than most.

reports.name: Cade Crossland
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the whole pitch and the walk rate is the problem. Across A+ & A this year, Crossland has punched out 118 batters over 81.3 innings, a 13.1 K/9 that translates to an MLB-equivalent 8.7, basically indistinguishable from what an average big-league arm produces, but the 7.0 BB/9 follows him through the conversion and lands at 6.8 while the MLB average sits at 3.2. That gap is what makes his 5.0 ERA and 1.5 WHIP feel honest rather than unlucky. If the control ever firms up enough to let the strikeout stuff breathe, he pitches his way into a back-end role; if it doesn't, the stuff alone produces a depth arm and nothing more.
